# How to Fill Kids Classes: 7 Practical Steps for Southern California Studios and Camps

Filling kids' classes comes down to seven habits: price clearly, discount only the seats about to expire, write listings that answer parents' real questions, run a waitlist, reply fast, keep your profile complete, and read your numbers. On ORYN Quest, joining and listing are free, and each step below pairs one platform feature with the plain practice that makes it work.

## 1. Set a Dollar Price Per Seat and Let the Platform Round Up to Credits

In the listing form, Class Cost is your dollar price per booked seat. The platform converts it to credits for families by rounding up, and you are paid that price less ORYN's agreed percentage, as set out in your vendor agreement. At today's rate, a $20 class shows families 20 credits.

Two practical notes follow from that setup. First, discounting never cuts your pay: promo codes, last-minute deals, and the sibling discount are paid for by ORYN, not out of your price. Second, families see only credits at checkout, so keep pricing decisions in the listing form rather than in chat.

How do you choose the number? Price for your local market, not your costs alone. A sensory-friendly gymnastics class in Pasadena with small ratios can sit well above the going rate for a large group class in the same ZIP, because parents pay for fit. Walk through your own neighborhood as a parent would: check what comparable classes charge, look at what your competitors include at that price, and round to a clean number. For broader demand tactics, our guide on [how to get more students for your kids' classes](https://orynquest.com/blog/how-to-get-more-students-for-kids-classes) goes deeper than pricing alone.

## 2. Switch On the Last-Minute Deal for Seats Within 24 Hours

Empty seats within 24 hours of a session are the hardest kind to fill, and a seat that goes unfilled earns nothing. A last-minute deal lets you offer 5 to 75% off sessions starting within 24 hours that still have open seats. ORYN pays the discount, so it never reduces your payout.

The sweet spot is a moderate discount on classes that would otherwise run with gaps: a swim session with three open lanes, an art class with spare easels, a camp day with unfilled seats. Seats booked earlier pay full price, and a class that fills early never shows a deal.

There is nothing to time or publish. Once you set a percentage on the listing, the deal applies on its own to each session in the 24 hours before it starts, so a weekday-morning class shows its deal from the morning before, including the evening hours when many families plan the next day. For the fuller playbook on moving empty inventory without touching your list price, see [how to fill open spots in a kids' class without discounting](https://orynquest.com/blog/how-to-fill-open-spots-in-a-kids-class).

## 3. Build a Listing That Tells Parents Everything They Need to Decide
![A classroom table set for a robotics class: a small robot car, spare wheels, a screwdriver, a cable and a laptop showing block code](/blog-assets/how-to-fill-a-kids-class-in-2026-5-booking-page-changes-that-s1-v2.jpg)


Parents book when they can quickly answer three questions: Is this right for my child's age? Can we get there and park? Will my child be comfortable? Fill in the optional fields that answer those questions: age range, skill level, total seats, and accessibility accommodations. Parents can filter for wheelchair-accessible and sensory-friendly listings, and those filters match the accommodations you list, so stating yours plainly helps the right families find you.

Photos do more heavy lifting than any paragraph. Show children mid-activity, faces engaged, space visible, and only with their parents' permission. A photo of a real class in action tends to do better than a stock image of a spotless empty room, because parents can read an empty room as an empty class. Aim for the full five photos: one wide shot of the space, two of activities in progress, one of the instructor engaging kids, and one that shows arrival or parking.

Add access and parking info even if it feels obvious. What is obvious to you, who drives there daily, is a decision point for a parent juggling two kids and a 4 p.m. window. Mention the things parents quietly worry about: where they park, whether siblings can wait nearby, what the drop-off handoff looks like. If the written parts stall you, our post on [writing a kids' class listing parents actually book](https://orynquest.com/blog/how-to-write-a-kids-class-listing-parents-book) walks through each section.

## 4. Run a Waitlist So Cancelled Seats Get Offered Automatically

Cancellations are a fact of kid life: fevers, birthday party invites, sibling conflicts. The waitlist offers each seat that opens up to the next family in line without any work from you. Turn it on per listing and set a maximum size (the default is 30). When a seat opens, the next family in line gets a 24-hour hold on it, and unused holds pass down the line automatically.

A waitlist also tells you something valuable about demand. A class with 15 enrolled and 12 waitlisted is underpriced or underscheduled: add a second time slot before you raise anything. A class with a waitlist of zero and seats open has a reach problem, not a pricing problem. Treat the list as free market research.

It helps to know the money side of cancellations. When a family gives up part of a booking by cancelling late or not showing up, that share is paid to you: a late cancel under 24 hours before class, or a no-show, pays your full payout. One honesty rule goes with it: a no-show may only be recorded for a child who did not come to a class that ran, and recording a false one breaks the Vendor Agreement.

## 5. Reply Within 30 Minutes and Send Post-Class Feedback

You get an email when a parent's message sits unread for 30+ minutes. Treat that threshold as your reply target. A parent who asks "is this class okay for a shy 5-year-old?" and gets an answer before dinner is more likely to book than one who waits two days. Reply speed is also one of the signals search ranking can depend on, along with parent satisfaction, completion and cancellation rates, and profile completeness.

Reviews follow the same logic. Only a parent with a completed booking can review, one review per booking on a 1-to-5-star scale, and families are asked 1 to 72 hours after class. Reply publicly to every review, especially the mixed ones, because parents read how you handle a complaint more carefully than the complaint itself. Name what went wrong, say what changed, and keep it short. Note the quality rule: with 3 or more reviews, an average below 4.0 stars puts a vendor on probation automatically. Listings stay visible, and the vendor comes off probation once the average is back at 4.0 or above.

After class, send the family short feedback on engagement, focus, social skills, and confidence, plus a note. A parent who reads "Maya shared materials with two new friends today" is more likely to rebook and tell friends. For discovery beyond the marketplace itself, our guide to [Google Business Profile for kids' activity businesses](https://orynquest.com/blog/google-business-profile-for-kids-activity-businesses) covers the local search essentials.

## 6. Keep Your Public Profile Complete

Visibility compounds. Keep your public profile complete with your logo, amenities, and social links, because parents cross-check before they book and a thin profile reads as a thin business. Profile completeness is also one of the signals search ranking can depend on. Use the same business name, address, and phone number on your profile, your website, and anywhere else families find you, so a parent who checks can tell it is the same place.

## 7. Use Your Dashboard to Spot What's Filling and What Isn't

The vendor dashboard and Revenue Report show earnings by month and by listing for completed sessions, plus a 6-month chart, quick insights, and category benchmarks that appear only when at least 5 other vendors share your category. No other vendor's individual numbers are ever shown.

Read the data in pairs. A listing with views but no bookings has a content problem: fix the photos, description, or price. A listing with neither views nor bookings has a discovery problem: fix the category, schedule, or search terms. If Tuesday 4 p.m. art fills and Wednesday 4 p.m. does not, stop running the empty slot and double down on the full one. Schedule discipline beats hope: every term, cut your two emptiest slots and add one more of whatever filled first.

On the money side, there is no fixed payout day. You are paid once a month through Stripe, for sessions completed at least 14 days earlier, when at least $50 is due; a smaller balance rolls over. ORYN pays the payout fee on that regular monthly payout, and an optional earlier payout carries a fee you see before you confirm. Each payout shows on your Payouts page with its status. Keep your own records alongside; you handle your own taxes, and for what that means, see the IRS Self-employed individuals tax center: https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/self-employed-individuals-tax-center.

## FAQ

### Does it cost anything to list classes on ORYN Quest?

Joining costs $0: no setup fee and no subscription. When families book, ORYN keeps an agreed percentage of the listed price. To apply, you confirm your business carries general liability insurance, and you handle your own taxes. ORYN issues tax forms such as 1099s where the law requires.

### Can I serve families outside Southern California?

Today ORYN Quest is open only for business ZIP codes starting 900 through 935, which covers Southern California. Businesses outside that range can join the vendor waiting list with a name, business, and area, and ORYN emails you when your area opens.

### What happens if a parent cancels at the last minute?

You get paid the share the family gave up. A cancel under 24 hours before class or a no-show pays your full payout, and a cancel 24 to 48 hours out pays half. If you cancel the session yourself before it starts, the family gets 100% back and you are not paid, and frequent cancelling can hurt your ranking.

### How fast do I need to reply to parent messages?

Aim for the 30-minute mark, the same threshold at which unread messages trigger an email to you. Reply speed is one of the signals search ranking can depend on, and it is often the difference between a booking and a parent moving on.
